content: Heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB) significantly affects the quality of life of otherwise healthy women. The perception of HMB is subjective, and its management depends on factors such as the severity of symptoms, the woman’s age, her desire for future pregnancies, and the presence of other medical conditions. Traditionally, HMB was defined as blood loss of 80 mL or more per menstrual cycle. However, the current definition is based on a woman’s perception of excessive bleeding that negatively impacts her quality of life. Intrauterine devices (IUDs) were initially developed as contraceptives. However, the addition of progestogens to these devices, such as the levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (LNG-IUS), has been shown to significantly reduce menstrual blood loss, with reductions of up to 90% reported by users. Despite its effectiveness, some women may find the insertion of the device invasive, which can affect its acceptability. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness, acceptability, and safety of progestogen-releasing intrauterine devices in reducing heavy menstrual bleeding. A comprehensive search of multiple databases and trial registries was conducted, including Cochrane Gynaecology and Fertility Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, and CINAHL, up to June 2019. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving women of reproductive age treated with LNG-IUS were included, comparing it to no treatment, placebo, or other medical or surgical therapies for HMB. A total of 25 RCTs involving 2,511 women were included in the analysis. Limitations in the evidence included a risk of attrition bias and a relatively small number of participants in some studies. LNG-IUS versus other medical therapies: The LNG-IUS may reduce menstrual blood loss, as measured by the alkaline haematin method (mean difference [MD] 66.91 mL, 95% confidence interval [CI] 42.61 to 91.20; low-certainty evidence) and the Pictorial Bleeding Assessment Chart (MD 55.05, 95% CI 27.83 to 82.28; low-certainty evidence). It is uncertain whether the LNG-IUS improves women’s satisfaction with treatment up to one year (relative risk [RR] 1.28, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.63; very low-certainty evidence). The LNG-IUS probably leads to a slightly higher quality of life compared to other medical therapies, as measured by the SF-36 (MD 2.90, 95% CI 0.06 to 5.74; moderate-certainty evidence) and the Menorrhagia Multi-Attribute Scale (MD 13.40, 95% CI 9.89 to 16.91; moderate-certainty evidence). Serious adverse events are probably similar between the LNG-IUS and other medical therapies (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.30; moderate-certainty evidence). Women using other medical therapies are more likely to discontinue treatment for any reason (RR 0.49, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.60; moderate-certainty evidence) and experience treatment failure compared to those using the LNG-IUS (RR 0.34, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.44; moderate-certainty evidence). LNG-IUS versus endometrial resection or ablation (EA): The results for bleeding outcomes were inconsistent. It is uncertain whether the LNG-IUS affects rates of amenorrhea (RR 1.21, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.72; low-certainty evidence), hypomenorrhea (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.33; low-certainty evidence), or eumenorrhea (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.30 to 1.00; very low-certainty evidence). It is uncertain whether satisfaction with treatment at 12 months differs between the LNG-IUS and EA (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.07; low-certainty evidence). The effect of the LNG-IUS on quality of life compared to EA is also uncertain (SF-36 MD −14.40, 95% CI −22.63 to −6.17; very low-certainty evidence). Women using the LNG-IUS are probably more likely to experience adverse events compared to those undergoing EA (RR 2.06, 95% CI 1.44 to 2.94; moderate-certainty evidence). Treatment failure, defined as persistent HMB or the need for additional treatment, may be more common with the LNG-IUS compared to EA at one year (RR 1.78, 95% CI 1.09 to 2.90; low-certainty evidence). The likelihood of requiring a hysterectomy may also be higher with the LNG-IUS at one year (RR 2.56, 95% CI 1.48 to 4.42; low-certainty evidence). LNG-IUS versus hysterectomy: It is uncertain whether the LNG-IUS affects HMB compared to hysterectomy (RR for amenorrhea 0.52, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.70; very low-certainty evidence). Satisfaction rates at five years may not differ significantly between the LNG-IUS and hysterectomy (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.08; low-certainty evidence). Quality of life outcomes, as measured by the SF-36, are also uncertain (MD 2.20, 95% CI −2.93 to 7.33; low-certainty evidence). Women using the LNG-IUS may be more likely to experience treatment failure requiring hysterectomy for HMB at one year compared to those who initially underwent hysterectomy (RR 48.18, 95% CI 2.96 to 783.22; low-certainty evidence). No cost data suitable for meta-analysis were reported in the included studies. Conclusions: The LNG-IUS may improve HMB and quality of life compared to other medical therapies. It appears to have similar effectiveness to endometrial destruction techniques for HMB, though it may result in more adverse events. The comparison between the LNG-IUS and hysterectomy remains uncertain due to very low-certainty evidence. Serious adverse events with the LNG-IUS are probably similar to those with other medical therapies, but adverse events are more likely compared to endometrial ablation.
